name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
title: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
answer: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology covers the conversion of CT, MRI and ultrasound volumes into physical objects: patient-specific replicas of bones, vessels, organs and tumours, plus surgical guides, implants and prosthetics. It sits alongside diagnostic imaging because the same scan data that supports a diagnosis can be segmented and printed for planning, consent or rehearsal. The work spans radiology departments, medical device manufacturing, maxillofacial and orthopaedic surgery, and academic anatomy teaching. Printed models are also used to explain a finding to a patient or a trainee when a screen image is hard to read.

sections.body: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology covers the conversion of CT, MRI and ultrasound volumes into physical objects: patient-specific replicas of bones, vessels, organs and tumours, plus surgical guides, implants and prosthetics. It sits alongside diagnostic imaging because the same scan data that supports a diagnosis can be segmented and printed for planning, consent or rehearsal. The work spans radiology departments, medical device manufacturing, maxillofacial and orthopaedic surgery, and academic anatomy teaching. Printed models are also used to explain a finding to a patient or a trainee when a screen image is hard to read.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The pipeline starts with a DICOM dataset from a scanner, usually a thin-slice CT or a high-resolution MRI. Segmentation software, including tools such as 3D Slicer and Materialise Mimics, separates the anatomy of interest from surrounding tissue, and a mesh is exported as STL or a comparable format. Printing itself uses material extrusion for cheap anatomical teaching models, vat photopolymerisation for smooth surgical guides, and powder bed fusion for titanium or cobalt chrome implants. A radiology department running this work needs a workstation with segmentation licences, a printer with its own ventilation and post-processing bench, and a quality record for every model that will touch a patient.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The radiologist or technologist selects the scan, checks slice thickness and contrast timing, and segments the target structure either by thresholding and region growing or by manual editing slice by slice. A surgeon or anatomist reviews the segmentation against the source images before the mesh is cleaned, hollowed and given connectors or split lines. The file is oriented, scaled to the patient, and printed in a material chosen for the job, rigid for bone, flexible for vessels, transparent for tumours near critical structures. Post-processing removes support material, and the finished model is measured against the original scan to confirm that dimensions match within the tolerance the clinical team set.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: A printed model used for diagnosis, surgical planning or an implant is a medical device in most jurisdictions, so it falls under the same quality system as any other device, including design controls, traceability and, for high-risk uses, premarket review. Patient scan data carries privacy obligations, and sending DICOM files to an external printing service is a data transfer that needs a lawful basis and a processing agreement.Provenance matters too: the version of the segmentation software, the printer, the material lot and the operator should all be recorded so a model can be reproduced or defended later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward segmentation models that produce printable meshes with less manual editing, and toward point-of-care printing inside the hospital rather than a central lab. That shift raises practical questions about who signs off on a model, how printers are validated and maintained, and how a department bills for the time. Regulatory frameworks for patient-specific devices are still being written in several countries, and the outcome of current liability cases may shape how much responsibility sits with the software vendor rather than the clinician. Teaching and consent uses will likely grow faster than implant uses because the risk profile is lower and the benefit to communication is immediate.
